line:
I step onto the quay, wring out my cloak, and meet the arbiter's eyes. "Madam, three of the Heron's Tithe's hands lie dead in our skiff, killed when they attacked us at the Gullspit light, and their master is a hooded man called Aldous, who sailed off with a man named Sparrow. May I give you the full account, and read Corvin's statement, indoors and by a fire?"

DM: also, is there any word yet on whether Corvin has signed his statement and named the man he called "H."?

input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~10:45 AM: his statement is signed and sealed with the arbiter. It names towns and dates for Elowen (Ashby Weir, then Lantern's Rest, then Saltmarsh) and says 'H.' is not Hale but 'Halloran Vey', a Saltmarsh shipping-factor who owns grey-sailed ships. Unverified; Corvin has asked to see Wren again. Wren has not yet read the statement herself beyond the summary.

input.description: Saltmarsh shipping-factor named as 'H.' in Corvin's signed statement (Day 10). Said to own grey-sailed ships including possibly the Heron's Tithe. Unverified: may be the Grey Cloak ('Aldous'), his employer, or a name Corvin chose to mislead.

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Halloran Vey; added 3 relationships to Halloran Vey

Your Persuasion check was a 19, even with exhaustion, and it lands. The arbiter looks at the three covered shapes in the skiff and at your soaked cloak, and says only, "Indoors. Fire. Now." Pell and two guards carry the dead to the hall's cold room. Kit goes with them, grey with weariness, to have her cuts seen to.

By the hall fire you give your account in full: the three hands who attacked at the Gullspit light, the hooded man called Aldous, Sparrow, the grey-sailed Heron's Tithe, and the lamp burning behind you. You ask for nothing and leave nothing out. The arbiter writes it all down. When you finish she sits back and says dryly, "Half of Saltmarsh watched that light come on, mistress. At least yours is an account that matches."

Now to your question. Yes, Corvin has signed. The statement lies sealed on her table, and she lets you read it. It names Ashby Weir, then Lantern's Rest, then Saltmarsh as the road he followed Elowen along, and the dates run to sixteen years back. Of "H." it says only this: not Hale, but a Saltmarsh shipping-factor, Halloran Vey, who owns grey-sailed ships. Whether that's the truth, a lie, or a name chosen to send you the wrong way, you can't tell from the page. The arbiter adds that Corvin has asked to see you again, and that she'll allow it with a guard at the door. It is nearly eleven.

You have no spell slots, Kit is hurt, and a squall is beating on the shutters. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~10 AM: per the arbiter, Corvin's dictated statement is finished and signed in his own hand, a clear account of Elowen (towns, dates: Ashby Weir, Lantern's Rest, the Wick-House). He has NOT yet named 'H.' or the smiling man; he told the clerk he will do so only to Wren. Still in the Vantry cellar.

entries.text:
Out of the story first, on your question. Yes, there's word. The arbiter says Corvin's statement is finished and signed in his own hand. It's a clear account of Elowen, with towns and dates: Ashby Weir, Lantern's Rest and the Wick-House. He has not named "H." or the smiling man in it. He told the clerk he would give that name to you and no one else, and the arbiter doesn't like it.

Now the story. You wring out your cloak, meet the arbiter's eyes, and give it plainly: three of the Heron's Tithe's hands dead in the skiff, killed when they attacked you at the Gullspit light, and their master a hooded man called Aldous, who sailed off with Sparrow. Your Persuasion check was a 16, even with exhaustion, and it lands. She doesn't question it. She looks at the covered shapes, then out at the white thread of the lamp, and her mouth tightens.

"That light has not burned in fifteen years," she says. "Half the quay thinks it a portent." She gives Pell a short order to see the dead carried to the Vantry mortuary, and turns back. "Come in out of the wet, both of you. There is a fire in the counting-room, and I will hear all of it, sitting down."

A little after ten you are dry-ish, with a bowl of broth, Kit asleep upright in her chair, and the arbiter's stylus scratching. She notes the name Aldous without comment, and Sparrow, and the grey cutter. When you finish, she reads Corvin's statement aloud. It is bleak and exact. Then she puts it down.

"He asks for you again," she says. "He says it concerns the name he promised. The cellar is below, and the guard will be at the door. It is your choice, mistress. You have your slots empty and your wits tired, and I cannot order you."

What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~10:30 AM: per the arbiter, Corvin dictated and signed his statement overnight. entries.text:
The arbiter takes in the three covered shapes, your sodden cloak and Kit's grey face. Your Persuasion check was a 9 with disadvantage. It doesn't charm her, but you hardly need to. "Indoors, yes," she says shortly. "The dead are the guard's business now. Pell, the hall's cellar, and a priest for them." She puts a dry cloak around Kit herself.

An hour later you sit by the Vantry hall's hearth with hot broth and give her everything: the three hands, the grey cutter, the hooded man Sparrow called master, the name "Aldous", and the lamp. She writes without interrupting. When you finish she sits quiet for a while.

Then she answers your question. Corvin dictated and signed his statement in the night, and the cellar clerk witnessed it. It names the towns and dates he knows for Elowen: Ashby Weir, the Wick-House, the Gullspit light. On "H.", he named only "a grey-sailed man I knew as Aldous", and swore he never learned another name. She watches you as she says it. "Either he was truthful or he lied well. You know him better than I do."

She will not hand you the full text until Dame Crowe's assize, but she has made you a sealed copy of the part that concerns your mother. It is half past ten. Your slots are empty and the squall still beats at the shutters.

What does Wren do?

It names Hale as 'H.' only in part: 'H.' is Master Hale's employer, a lord's steward who serves 'the man called Aldous'; Corvin says he sold Aldous forged pedigrees through Hale for years and that Aldous wanted Elowen's lamp, not the ledger. entries.text:
The quay is loud with rain, gulls and the bell, and the arbiter's eyes go from the covered shapes in the skiff to your soaked cloak. You give your account plainly: three hands attacked you at the Gullspit light, their master is a hooded man called Aldous, and he left with a man named Sparrow. Your Persuasion check was a 20, even with exhaustion, and it lands. She orders the dead carried to the guardhouse for the coroner. "A hall that has the lamp burning across its water," she says dryly, "had best hear the whole of it indoors." She takes you and Kit to the Vantry hall, where a fire is already lit in the counting-room, and has dry blankets brought.

As for your question, yes. Corvin has signed. Pell brings the statement, three sheets in a clerk's hand, with Corvin's neat signature at the foot and the cellar guard's witness mark beside it. You read it by the fire.

It says he sold forged pedigrees for years through a steward he calls "H." and that he now names: Hale, Lord Edric's own steward, who was only ever the go-between. Hale's employer is the man called Aldous. Corvin writes that Aldous never cared about the ledger. What he wanted, from the very first, was Elowen's lamp. Corvin swears he doesn't know who Aldous really is or where he lives, and that he last met him on the grey cutter. That is as far as the page goes, and it reads like a man telling the truth with a lie or two folded in, which is how Corvin always told it.

A note in a different hand is pinned to the last sheet. Corvin asks to speak with you again before the assize, in the cellar, when you are rested.

It's half past ten. You are damp, warmed by the fire, without spell slots, and with a hearing and a night's sleep still ahead. What does Wren do?

She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level. At level 2: Bardic Inspiration die d6.
Jack of All Trades: Starting at 2nd level, you can add half your proficiency bonus, rounded down, to any ability check you make that doesn't already include your proficiency bonus.

Song of Rest (d6): Beginning at 2nd level, you can use soothing music or oration to help revitalize your wounded allies during a short rest. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Spells known are fixed until a level-up.
